client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester — the coursework is just so much harder than I expected, and I feel like I'm constantly falling behind no matter how hard I try. It's gotten to the point where I've basically stopped hanging out with my friends because I feel like I should be studying, but then I just end up sitting alone feeling awful about everything. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I'm genuinely glad you gave it a shot. What you're describing — that exhausting cycle of isolating yourself to study, then feeling worse and not really studying anyway — makes so much sense as a response to feeling overwhelmed, and it doesn't mean anything is wrong with you. I'm curious: when you're sitting alone feeling awful, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind about yourself or your situation?

client: Honestly, the thoughts that go through my head are pretty brutal. It's mostly like... "everyone else is handling this fine, why can't you?" and then I start thinking about how I've wasted the whole day and I'm falling further behind, which just makes me freeze up even more. And then there's this guilt about not calling my family back, not responding to texts, like I'm failing at everything all at once.
therapist: Those thoughts sound exhausting and really painful — that sense of failing on every front at once can feel absolutely crushing. I want to gently point something out: the thought "everyone else is handling this fine" is something your mind is presenting as a fact, but I wonder how much real evidence you actually have for that, versus it being an assumption that's filling in the blanks. What do you think — is there any part of you that suspects other students might be struggling more than they let on?

client: I mean... yeah, maybe. I know logically that people don't exactly post about their breakdowns on Instagram, but it still *feels* like everyone else has it together when I'm sitting in the library at midnight completely falling apart. It's hard to shake that feeling even when part of me knows it might not be the full picture.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you noticed the gap between what you *know* logically and what your mind *feels* in that vulnerable midnight moment, and that awareness is actually the first step in loosening the grip those thoughts have on you. That feeling is so convincing partly because when we're struggling, we tend to compare our messy insides to everyone else's polished outsides, which will almost always make us come up short. When you're in that library late at night and the thought hits hardest, what do you think it would feel like to gently remind yourself that you're only seeing other people's highlight reels?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like, yeah, nobody posts about crying in their dorm room at 2am. But when I'm actually sitting there in the library and that feeling hits, it's so overwhelming that I can't imagine having the mental space to stop and think "oh, this is just their highlight reel." It feels less like a thought I can reason with and more like a wave that just knocks me over before I even see it coming.
therapist: That "wave" image you used is really powerful and honestly quite accurate — when emotions hit that intensity, the thinking brain genuinely does get flooded, so it's not a personal failing that logic flies out the window in those moments. Rather than trying to reason with the wave while it's crashing over you, it might be more helpful to think about what small anchor — even just one tiny thing — could give you a moment of footing before it fully takes over. I'm wondering, when you're in that overwhelmed state in the library, is there anything, even something small like a text to a friend or stepping outside for a minute, that has ever helped even slightly?

client: Honestly, stepping outside has crossed my mind before, but I always feel like I can't because everyone will notice I'm leaving and think I'm falling apart or can't handle the workload. There's this pressure to just sit there and look like I have it together, even when I'm completely drowning inside. So even that small thing feels kind of impossible in the moment.
therapist: It's so telling that even a potentially helpful escape route gets blocked by that same fear — "everyone is watching and judging me" — which suggests this thought pattern is really working overtime to keep you stuck and isolated. And I want to reflect something back gently: the very act of sitting there forcing yourself to look okay while drowning is costing you enormously, so in a way the thing you're doing to protect yourself from judgment might actually be making everything harder. What do you imagine would *actually* happen — not what the anxious part of your brain predicts, but what would realistically occur — if someone did notice you stepping outside for a few minutes?

client: Honestly, if I really think about it... most people would probably just assume I needed some air or had to take a call or something. But the anxious part of my brain is so loud that it's almost impossible to believe that in the moment — it feels like stepping out would be this huge announcement that something is wrong with me. And I guess I know logically you're right, but knowing something and actually feeling it are two completely different things.
therapist: You've just articulated one of the most important insights in understanding how anxiety works — that gap between knowing and *feeling* is real, and it's not a sign you're doing something wrong, it's just how our brains are wired under stress. Rather than trying to close that gap all at once, what if we thought of stepping outside not as something you have to *believe* is safe first, but as a small experiment — doing it once just to see what actually happens, and letting the evidence speak for itself? What do you think — is there a part of you that might be willing to try that, even with the anxiety still present?

client: I mean... I guess there's a small part of me that can see the logic in that, like treating it as an experiment rather than something I have to be fully on board with emotionally. But I'm worried that even if I do it and nothing bad happens, my brain will just find some reason to dismiss it, like "well that time was fine but next time could be different." It feels like the anxiety always has a comeback, you know?
therapist: You've just described something really sharp about how anxiety operates — it's like a defense attorney that can always find a counterargument, and that's genuinely frustrating. But here's something worth sitting with: the fact that you can *anticipate* anxiety's comeback means part of you is already one step ahead of it, which is actually a form of power even if it doesn't feel that way yet. What do you think it would mean for you if, over time, you started collecting a whole series of these small experiments where nothing bad happened — do you think eventually the evidence might start to feel harder for anxiety to dismiss?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that could work. But honestly, anxiety is really good at just... moving the goalposts. Like, even if I go to that social event and nothing bad happens, it'll just say "well, you got lucky this time" or "next time will be different," and I'm back to square one.
therapist: You're absolutely right that anxiety is a master at moving the goalposts, and I don't want to minimize how exhausting it is to feel like you can never quite win that argument with it. But I want to gently reframe something — the goal of these experiments isn't necessarily to *silence* anxiety, but to slowly build a relationship with yourself where you take small actions *despite* it being loud, which over time shifts something deeper than just having evidence. I'm curious, when you think about your life right now, is there a version of you you can imagine who isn't free of anxiety, but is just a little less controlled by it — and what might that look like?

client: I mean... maybe. I can kind of picture someone who still feels anxious at work but doesn't spend three hours before a meeting rehearsing every possible way it could go wrong. But honestly, even imagining that version of me feels a little foreign, like I'm describing someone else's life, not mine.
therapist: The fact that you *can* picture that version of you, even if it feels distant, is genuinely meaningful — it means some part of you holds that possibility, even if anxiety has made it feel like someone else's story for now. That image you described — still anxious but not spending three hours rehearsing worst-case scenarios — is actually a really concrete and honest goal, not some perfect anxiety-free life, just a little more freedom. I'm wondering, when you think about that version of you, what's one small thing that feels different about how they treat themselves compared to how you treat yourself right now?

client: I think that version of me... probably doesn't immediately assume they did something wrong when someone doesn't text back right away. Like right now, if a friend goes quiet for a day or two, I spiral into thinking I said something offensive or that they're pulling away, and I'll replay every recent conversation looking for what I messed up. That other version of me seems like they could just... let it sit without it becoming this whole investigation.
therapist: That's such a vivid and specific example, and it tells me a lot about how much energy you're spending as a kind of constant self-monitor, always scanning for evidence that you've done something wrong. What's worth noticing is that the investigation you described — replaying every conversation — isn't actually protecting you from anything, it's just anxiety dressed up as problem-solving, keeping you busy while making you feel worse. When a friend goes quiet and that urge to investigate kicks in, what do you think the anxiety is most afraid will happen if you *don't* go looking for what you did wrong?
